title: Calm in the Character of God: Omnipresence and Anxiety
speaker: Elder Nick Anderson
series: Calm in the Character of God

outline.title: The Doctrine of Omnipresence
subpoints: God is present everywhere at all times, distinct from pantheism and deism.
God actively sustains the universe; creation ceases without His presence.
No place exists where God is absent, as affirmed in Psalm 139.

outline.title: God as a Present Help in Trouble
subpoints: Psalm 46 declares God is a 'very present help' and refuge.
Believers need not fear cosmic or earthly upheavals because God is with them.
The Lord of Hosts is a warrior and commander who provides strength.

outline.title: Human Weakness and Divine Strength
subpoints: The Christian life is impossible by human strength alone.
Scriptural examples (Moses, David, Daniel) show God accomplishing the impossible.
Paul’s testimony: strength is perfected in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:10).

outline.title: Case Study: Elisha’s Servant
subpoints: The servant saw only the threatening Assyrian army.
Elisha trusted that those with them were more than those against them.
God opened the servant’s eyes to see the spiritual reality of divine protection.

outline.title: Application: Faith Over Fear
subpoints: Anxiety is a response to circumstances; faith is a response to God’s character.
Philippians 4:5 grounds the command to be anxious for nothing in the nearness of the Lord.
Believers are called to cast burdens on God and trust His sustaining power.

summary:
In this concluding lesson of the series 'Calm in the Character of God,' Elder Nick Anderson explores the doctrine of God’s omnipresence as a source of comfort for the anxious heart. He distinguishes the biblical view of God’s presence from pantheism and deism, emphasizing that God is actively sustaining every moment of creation. By examining Psalm 139, the sermon highlights that there is no place where God is absent, offering ultimate comfort to the believer and terror to the unbeliever.

The teaching further addresses the human tendency to rely on self-sufficiency, contrasting it with the biblical truth that the Christian life is impossible without divine strength. Using examples from the Old Testament and the apostle Paul’s writings, the sermon illustrates that God often brings circumstances beyond human capacity to foster trust in His power. The narrative of Elisha’s servant in 2 Kings 6 serves as a central illustration, showing how spiritual sight reveals God’s protective presence even when physical circumstances appear threatening.

The sermon concludes by urging believers to choose faith over fear, grounding their peace in the nearness of the Lord as described in Philippians 4. By recognizing God as a 'very present help in trouble' (Psalm 46), Christians are called to cast their burdens on Him, trusting that He is the Lord of Hosts who sustains and protects His people.
